findings.fix: Preserve John's love-of-the-Father wording without making the ambiguous genitive a one-direction possessive gloss.
findings.before: Loving pleasure rather than God corresponds to John's contrast between loving the world and the Father's love. John specifies worldly desires and their passing; Timothy's list also names betrayal, recklessness and conceit. Pleasure and world are not treated as identical printed categories.
findings.after: Loving pleasure rather than God corresponds to John's contrast between loving the world and the love of the Father. John specifies worldly desires and their passing; Timothy's list also names betrayal, recklessness and conceit. Pleasure and world are not treated as identical printed categories.
findings.resolution: Applied the same rationale-only refinement to the current final primary and matching chapters3–4 contribution; all source outcomes and target IDs remain unchanged.

findings.fix: Do not turn the women's being led by desires into an explicitly stated method used by both texts' teachers; keep Peter's own-slavery role clear.
findings.before: Both describe deceptive people gaining control through desires. Peter names enticement and slavery to corruption; Timothy's letter names entering houses and taking captive particular weak women burdened with sins. It neither extends that description to all women nor supplies an unprinted sexual act.
findings.after: Both place captivity or enticement alongside desires. Peter explicitly names enticing through fleshly desires and the teachers' own slavery to corruption; Timothy's letter names entering houses and taking captive particular weak women described as led by various desires. It does not independently state every method of gaining control, extend that description to all women or supply an unprinted sexual act.
findings.resolution: Applied the same rationale-only refinement to the current final primary and matching chapters3–4 contribution; all source outcomes and target IDs remain unchanged.
